title: Jazz Party trumpet section, Dizzy brought in for discipline and the two bass players
summary: Duke called Dizzy in when his trumpet players were missing, and hired a second bassist because Ragland drank.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: I think it was on, "Jazz Party," the record, "Jazz Party," that I was on with the band, Quentin Jackson, Butter as we called him, told me -- it was on some

things there was no first trumpet part, and so Duke had -- it was a double date, you know. One date, then we had dinner, then we came back and did the second one, and when we came back, Duke had told Bobby Boyd, the road manager, you know, to go get Dizzy Gillespie, because he wanted some discipline. And he got it. When Dizzy walked in the studio, everybody was sitting up like tin soldiers, you know? But now Clarke Terry didn't have to worry about it, you know, because Clarke could handle himself. And that was one of the best trumpet sections that Duke had. He had Clarke Terry, Shorty Baker, Ray Nance and Cat Anderson.
That's a hell of a section.

Yeah. But they weren't there on the first part of the date, you know. So Duke just said, well, he wanted to be sure he had another trombone player, -- or, a trumpet player, so he called Dizzy in. But by that time he had five trumpets, you know?

But everybody had to play and pay attention. Like there was another time when Duke said -- he had two bass players. He had Junior Ragland and Al Lucas, but Junior Ragland would get drunk, so Duke said, 'I'd better hire another bass player so I can be sure I have one.'
So Al and Ragland started going out and
Duke said, 'Gee, I'm paying two bass players and neither one of them are here.'
Oh, boy, that was a very comical scene, you know, in a lot of ways. But musically, that was my favorite orchestra.
